paper.page: SPI: Query-Depth-Adaptive Indexing for Streaming RAG in Vector Databases Dong Liu Yale University New Haven, CT, USA dong.liu@aya.yale.edu Yanxuan Yu Columbia University New York, NY, USA yy3523@columbia.edu ABSTRACT Vector databases (VecDBs) are increasingly deployed in retrieval- augmented generation (RAG) pipelines where query processing and document ingestion occur concurrently. The index layer needs to provide low-latency search while incorporating new vectors with- out frequent global rebuilding. Existing VecDB pipelines typically operate within a uniform representation regime, despite substantial variation in the semantic granularity required across queries. This motivates an index design that supports incremental updates while adapting retrieval depth to query distribution and complexity. We propose Semantic Pyramid Indexing (SPI), a VecDB-layer indexing framework that organizes embeddings into 𝐿 semantically aligned resolution levels and selects retrieval depth per query using a lightweight uncertainty-aware controller. SPI supports progres- sive coarse-to-fine ANN search, level-wise streaming insertion with- out global rebuilding, and distributed execution through LSH-based partitioning with asynchronous coordination. Unlike hierarchical ANN structures with fixed traversal rules (e.g., SPANN), SPI adapts resolution at query time while remaining compatible with FAISS and Qdrant backends. On MS MARCO and Natural Questions, SPI achieves competitive Recall@10 with lower latency under the same dense encoder family, yielding a 1.4–2.3× average retrieval latency reduction under fixed Recall@10 targets relative to comparable approximate-ANN base- lines. A prototype scaling study up to 8 nodes shows 6.2× through- put scaling (≈73% efficiency); the 16-node configuration is included for completeness but shows diminishing efficiency. We provide a top-𝐾 stability guarantee: queries with sufficient retrieval margin return an identical top-𝐾 set at a shallower level. Code and config- urations are available at https://github.com/FastLM/SPI_VecDB. PVLDB Reference Format: Dong Liu and Yanxuan Yu. The pyramid organizes document embeddings at multiple representational depth levels (all levels index the same document corpus; levels differ in semantic discrim- inability). Incoming streaming queries are routed to the ap- propriate depth by a lightweight controller, enabling early- exit search for simple queries and deep-representation search for complex ones. 1 INTRODUCTION Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are increasingly deployed in streaming settings where queries arrive continuously alongside live document ingestion [28]. Production vector databases (VecDBs) such as Milvus, Qdrant, and Weaviate must serve these workloads at low latency while keeping indices fresh—a regime where static, single-resolution indexing structures become a bottle- neck: they either over-spend on complex queries or under-serve simple ones. The problem. Existing RAG retrieval pipelines commit every query to a single semantic resolution—flat, HNSW, or product- quantized indices embed all documents uniformly and require ex- haustive ANN search over a fixed embedding space. This design ignores a fundamental asymmetry in query complexity: a broad query like “Who discovered gravity?” is reliably answered by a shallow, high-entropy embedding that excels at broad topical sepa- ration, while “Equation in Newton’s third-law paper” demands a deep, discriminative embedding that can distinguish closely related passages. Here, “resolution” refers to the semantic discriminability of the embedding space—the ability of the embedding to separate relevant from non-relevant documents—not to the granularity of indexed information units. All pipeline variants index at the docu- ment level; the difference is in how much representational depth is devoted to encoding subtle semantic distinctions. Forcing both simple and complex queries through the same single-resolution index wastes compute on the former and may under-resolve the 1 arXiv:2511.16681v3 [cs.CL] 14 Jun 2026

latter. Under streaming workloads, the problem compounds: insert- ing new documents into a flat or clustered index either blocks live queries (rebuild cost) or degrades index quality (lazy append). Our approach. We propose Semantic Pyramid Indexing (SPI), a representation-depth-adaptive indexing layer for streaming RAG in vector databases. As shown in Figure 1, SPI constructs an 𝐿-level semantic pyramid over the same document corpus, where level 1 uses shallow broad-scope embeddings and level 𝐿 uses deep fine- grained embeddings trained to maximize per-query discriminability via lightweight residual refinement encoders. At query time, a com- pact uncertainty-aware controller predicts the minimum resolution level sufficient for reliable retrieval, and parallel distributed search is launched across nodes partitioned by the pyramid structure. Doc- uments arriving in the stream are inserted level-by-level without invalidating existing pyramid levels, maintaining semantic consis- tency under continuous ingestion. This design makes three concrete contributions over prior work. First, unlike hierarchical indices that use fixed traversal rules, SPI targets a complementary design point: reducing average retrieval cost by routing queries to the minimum representation depth needed for stable top-𝑘 retrieval. Second, by co-designing the index layout with distributed parallel execution, SPI achieves throughput scal- ing that grows proportionally with cluster size up to 8 nodes (79% efficiency) under bursty streaming arrivals. Third, SPI provides a top-𝐾 stability guarantee (Theorem 1): queries whose top-𝐾 neigh- borhood has sufficient retrieval margin retrieve exactly the same top-𝐾 set at a shallower level, so early termination is exact for those queries; the margin condition also explains when it is not. Contributions. • SPI framework: a query-adaptive, multi-resolution index- ing framework supporting streaming ingestion in parallel VecDB deployments. • Theoretical guarantees: recall preservation and per-query latency bounds under adaptive resolution control with stream- ing updates. • Empirical evaluation: experiments on MS MARCO and Natural Questions show competitive Recall@10 with lower retrieval latency, while streaming and scaling studies eval- uate insertion overhead and parallel throughput. 2 RELATED WORK SPI sits at the intersection of ANN indexing, streaming vector databases, and retrieval-augmented generation. 2.1 ANN Indexing in Vector Databases Classical ANN foundations include LSH [1], product quantiza- tion [8, 16], and graph indices such as HNSW [21]. Billion-scale systems combine these with pruning and hybrid memory/disk lay- outs: ScaNN [10], DiskANN [15], SPANN [4]. GPU-accelerated indices including CAGRA [25] and ParlayANN [22] further ad- vance throughput via massive parallelism. Production VecDBs— Milvus [28], Qdrant [27], Pinecone [29]—integrate these backends with distributed storage and query execution. SPI relationship. Each SPI pyramid level is a standard FAISS IVF-PQ or Qdrant HNSW index [5]. SPI adds a semantic resolution layer above these backends; it is orthogonal to the specific ANN algorithm used at each level. CAGRA or DiskANN could replace FAISS at any level without changing SPI’s control logic. 2.2 Streaming and Dynamic ANN Several recent systems address streaming vector index updates. FreshDiskANN [14] introduced soft deletions and periodic batch consolidation for graph-based ANN. IP-DiskANN [31] eliminates batch consolidation via in-place insertion/deletion on DiskANN, achieving stable recall without rebuilds. Quake [23] takes a comple- mentary approach: adaptive partition scanning that adjusts index structure and query parameters to workload shifts in a NUMA- aware manner, achieving 1.5–38× lower query latency over HNSW/DiskANN on dynamic workloads. VStream [9] is a distributed streaming vec- tor search system that introduces hot–cold separation and dynamic partitioning for streaming workloads, achieving 251–373× query efficiency gains over batch-mode systems. SPI relationship. These systems address geometric index fresh- ness: how to update graph connectivity or partition balance without recall degradation. SPI addresses a complementary axis: even given a perfectly fresh index, uniform-resolution ANN still wastes com- pute on simple queries. SPI’s streaming insertion is append-only (no graph repair), trading eventual consistency at finer levels for minimal per-insert latency. The two approaches are directly com- posable: SPI’s level-1 index could be backed by IP-DiskANN or Quake. 2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation RAG couples dense or sparse retrievers with generative readers [12, 17, 20]. Strong retrievers include ANCE [30], Contriever [11], SPLADE- v2 [6], ColBERTv2 [26], and HyDE [7]. End-to-end RAG systems such as Atlas [13] jointly train retrievers and readers. Semantic caching [2] and FrugalGPT [3] reduce inference cost but treat re- trieval granularity as a pipeline configuration. SPI moves query- adaptive resolution control into the VecDB index layer itself. 2.4 Comparison with Existing Approaches Table 1 contrasts SPI with representative systems across key dimen- sions. To clar- ify SPI’s positioning at the boundary between retriever learning 2

and database systems, we begin with an explicit separation of its two phases. Two-phase architecture. SPI operates in two distinct phases with different system roles: • Phase 1 — Offline encoder training (retriever learning). Given a training corpus, learn 𝐿−1 refinement encoders {𝑓 ℓ , 𝑔 ℓ } 𝐿 ℓ=2 via joint contrastive training (Section 3.5). This is a one-time, corpus-specific cost analogous to fine-tuning DPR or ColBERT. The output is a set of encoder checkpoints. • Phase 2 — Online index system (VecDB layer). Given the trained encoders, build and maintain the 𝐿-level index {I (ℓ ) } 𝐿 ℓ=1 , serve live queries via progressive retrieval and the controller, handle streaming insertions without rebuilds, and distribute exe- cution across nodes. This phase is the core database contribution of SPI. The two phases are decoupled: Phase 2 can accept any encoder that produces compatible embeddings—a practitioner who already has a multi-resolution encoder (e.g., from MRL pre-training) can adopt the SPI index without retraining. Conversely, the encoder from Phase 1 could be plugged into a flat FAISS index, but would forfeit the system-level gains of Phase 2. SPI’s claimed contributions span both phases, and we evaluate them separately (single-node quality in Q1 reflects Phase 1+2; distributed scaling in Q3 reflects Phase 2 alone). Notation. 𝑏 max , 𝑏 1 · 2 ℓ −1  , 𝑏 1 = 8, 𝑏 max = 32, so (𝑏 1 , . . . , 𝑏 𝐿 ) = (8, 16, 32, 32, . . . ) for any 𝐿. This matches Figure 2, where queries enter at level 1 and descend only as far as the controller deems necessary. 3.1 Design Rationale and Overview SPI treats retrieval as a progressive representation-depth search. Un- like classical hierarchical indices where levels partition documents at different granularities (document, passage, sentence), SPI always indexes documents as atomic units; what varies across levels is the semantic discriminability of the embedding space. Formally, e (ℓ ) 𝑑 is trained to maximise Δ ℓ (𝑞)—the similarity margin between relevant and non-relevant documents—so that deeper levels refine fine-grained relational distinctions rather than changing the unit of retrieval. In a streaming deployment, pyramid levels are populated on- demand: D (ℓ ) (𝑡) = {𝑑 | 𝑡 arr 𝑑 + 𝑇 (ℓ −1) ins ≤ 𝑡 } , with 𝑇 (0) ins =0, yielding Figure 2: Distributed SPI: queries enter at level 1 (coarsest) and descend only as far as semantically necessary. Each level is independently indexed across 𝑁 distributed partitions. D (1) (𝑡) ⊇ · · · ⊇ D (𝐿) (𝑡) at every instant 𝑡. A document is avail- able at level 1 within the base encoding latency 𝑇 (1) enc ; it ascends to level ℓ after asynchronous refinement within lag 𝑇 (ℓ ) ins . Queries in the interim are served at the deepest currently available level, incurring a bounded recall cost rather than missing the document entirely. Precision-scaled quantization. Complementing the representa- tional hierarchy, SPI assigns quantization precision 𝑏 ℓ to each level’s stored embeddings via the schedule defined in Notation. The design principle is: • Shallow levels need compression: level 1 searches the full corpus D with pool size 𝑁 1 ; storage dominates and coarser quantization is acceptable since broad discrimination tolerates larger 𝛿 1 . • Deep levels need precision: level ℓ searches a refined pool of size 𝑁 ℓ ≪ 𝑁 1 ; storage overhead is negligible, so FP32 precision pre- serves the fine-grained discriminability gained by deeper en- coders. The quantization error at level ℓ is bounded by 𝛿 ℓ ≤ ∥e∥ ∞ 2 𝑏 ℓ −1 . The precision schedule ensures 𝛿 ℓ · Δ ℓ (𝑞) ≪ 𝜏 for all ℓ, so quantiza- tion errors do not shift any query’s optimal stopping level. The total stored memory for the 𝐿-level pyramid is 𝑀 store = |D| · 𝐿 ∑︁ ℓ=1 𝐷 ℓ · 𝑏 ℓ 8 bytes, while the active working memory per query is 𝑀 active (𝑞) = ℓ final (𝑞) ∑︁ ℓ=1 𝑁 ℓ · 𝐷 ℓ · 𝑏 ℓ 8 bytes, which is dominated by the level-1 term 𝑁 1 𝐷 1 𝑏 1 /8 and decreases geometrically with ℓ because both 𝑁 ℓ and 𝐷 ℓ contract across levels. SPI therefore operates in three stages: (1) construction of a semantic pyramid where each level provides progressively finer- grained representational discriminability; (2) progressive distributed retrieval that re-scores candidates at increasing representation depth; and (3) query-adaptive depth selection via a lightweight uncertainty-aware controller (as shown in Figure 2). 3

3.2 Semantic Pyramid Index ≠ Hierarchical Index Although SPI employs multiple resolution levels, it is fundamentally different from traditional hierarchical ANN indices (e.g., HNSW, SPANN). Existing hierarchical indices organize data to accelerate geometric nearest-neighbor search via static partitioning, fixed traversal rules, or manually tuned thresholds. SPI introduces a semantic hierarchy: each level corresponds to a learned abstraction of meaning, and traversal depth is decided per query by a learned controller—not by fixed heuristics. SPI therefore should be viewed as a progressive semantic retrieval framework that generalizes beyond specific ANN backends. 3.3 Query Complexity and Optimal Resolution Retrieval queries differ in the semantic granularity required to separate relevant from irrelevant documents. SPI formalizes this via the expected similarity gap at level ℓ: Δ ℓ (𝑞) = E 𝑑 + h sim(q (ℓ ) , e (ℓ ) 𝑑 + ) i − E 𝑑 − h sim(q (ℓ ) , e (ℓ ) 𝑑 − ) i , where 𝑑 + and 𝑑 − are relevant and non-relevant documents. The optimal level for query 𝑞 is: ℓ ∗ (𝑞) = min { ℓ | Δ ℓ (𝑞) ≥ 𝜏 } , where 𝜏 is a task-dependent separability threshold. Directly evalu- ating ℓ ∗ (𝑞) is infeasible; SPI approximates it from the coarse query embedding q (1) . 3.4 Multi-Resolution Semantic Pyramid Construction For each document 𝑑, SPI constructs a tower of 𝐿 embeddings {e (1) 𝑑 , . . . , e (𝐿) 𝑑 } with a monotonically decreasing dimension sched- ule 𝐷 1 ≥ 𝐷 2 ≥ · · · ≥ 𝐷 𝐿 > 0: • Level 1 (base): e (1) 𝑑 ∈ R 𝐷 1 is the output of a frozen Contriever encoder [11] (𝐷 1 =768). • Levels ℓ = 2, . . . , 𝐿 (refinement): e (ℓ ) 𝑑 ∈ R 𝐷 ℓ is produced by a patch-Transformer refinement encoder 𝑓 ℓ , described below. In our 𝐿=3 setup: (𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , 𝐷 3 ) = (768, 512, 256). Patch-Transformer architecture for 𝑓 ℓ . A standard Transformer expects a sequence of tokens, not a single vector. To apply Trans- former attention over an embedding e ∈ R 𝐷 ℓ −1 , we split it into 𝐾 non-overlapping patches of dimension 𝑝 = 𝐷 ℓ −1 /𝐾: e ↦ −→ [e 1:𝑝 , e 𝑝+1:2𝑝 , . . . , e (𝐾 −1)𝑝+1:𝐾𝑝 ] ∈ R 𝐾 ×𝑝 . A learnable [CLS] token is prepended, forming a (𝐾 + 1)-token se- quence. Two Transformer encoder blocks (multi-head self-attention with 𝐻 =4 heads, hidden dim 𝑝, pre-LayerNorm, GELU activation) are applied, and the [CLS] output is projected linearly to R 𝐷 ℓ . In our experiments: level 2 uses 𝐾=12, 𝑝=64, projecting to 512; level 3 uses 𝐾=8, 𝑝=64, projecting to 256. Total parameters per 𝑓 ℓ : ≈4M (attention) + 1M (projection) = 5M. Self-attention over the 𝐾 patches allows 𝑓 ℓ to recombine infor- mation across different regions of the input embedding before com- pressing it—a strictly richer operation than an MLP projection. Why compression can increase discriminability. The dimension reduction 𝐷 ℓ < 𝐷 ℓ −1 appears to discard information, but the super- vision signal reverses this intuition. Each 𝑓 ℓ is trained with InfoNCE contrastive loss on the hard negatives that level ℓ−1 failed to sepa- rate—i.e., the query-document pairs for which Δ ℓ −1 (𝑞) < 𝜏. This curriculum forces 𝑓 ℓ to concentrate task-relevant directions into 𝐷 ℓ dimensions while discarding the low-discriminability variance that dominates 𝐷 ℓ −1 . The mechanism is analogous to Matryoshka Representation Learning [18], where supervised training provably improves task discriminability of lower-dimensional subspaces. Formally, after training, Δ ℓ (𝑞) ≥ Δ ℓ −1 (𝑞) for the queries routed to level ℓ, which is a necessary condition for recall preservation (Theorem 1). All 𝐿−1 refinement encoders {𝑓 ℓ } 𝐿 ℓ=2 are trained jointly (Sec- tion 3.5); there are no separate pretrained checkpoints for ℓ ≥ 2. Query-side encoding. Each document encoder 𝑓 ℓ has a symmetric but separate query encoder 𝑔 ℓ with the same patch-Transformer architecture (independent parameters). Document and query en- coders do not share weights, following standard dual-encoder de- sign [17]. Unlike document encoding (which is asynchronous and pre-computed), query encoding is fully synchronous: q (ℓ ) = 𝑔 ℓ (q (ℓ −1) ) is computed on-the-fly at query time, triggered only if the controller decides to proceed to level ℓ. All 𝑔 ℓ are cached on GPU memory; the per-level query encoding cost is 8.1 ms (level 1, Contriever), 3.9 ms (level 2), and 1.8 ms (level 3)—decreasing because deeper query encoders operate on smaller candidate sets and the patches are smaller. This asymmetry (async documents, sync queries) is a key operational property: document encoding never blocks queries, and query encoding cost is bounded by Í ℓ final ℓ=1 𝑇 𝑞,ℓ enc , which equals 15.1 ms for level-1-exit queries and at most 24.9 ms for level-3 queries. Higher-level embeddings are defined by the residual refinement: e (ℓ ) 𝑑 = 𝑓 ℓ (e (ℓ −1) 𝑑 ) + W ℓ e (1) 𝑑 , ℓ ≥ 2, where W ℓ ∈ R 𝐷 ℓ ×𝐷 1 is a learned residual alignment matrix that anchors every level to the base semantic space, preventing semantic drift across levels. Each level is indexed independently across 𝑁 distributed partitions: I (ℓ ) = 𝑁 Ø 𝑖=1 Index
{e (ℓ ) 𝑑 | 𝑑 ∈ D 𝑖 }  . 3.5 Progressive Encoding and Joint Training All refinement encoders {𝑓 ℓ } 𝐿 ℓ=2 are trained jointly to enforce cross- level semantic alignment. Training optimizes: L total = 𝐿 ∑︁ ℓ=1 𝛼 ℓ L (ℓ ) retrieval + 𝛽L consistency + 𝛾 L reg , where L (ℓ ) retrieval is an in-batch InfoNCE contrastive loss, and L consistency = 𝐿−1 ∑︁ ℓ=1 ∥e (ℓ ) 𝑑 − proj ℓ (e (ℓ+1) 𝑑 )∥ 2 2 (1) penalizes semantic drift between adjacent levels. We set 𝛼 ℓ = 1/𝐿 uniformly, 𝛽 = 0.5, 𝛾 = 0.01 (weight decay); these values are fixed across all experiments and are not dataset-specific. 4

sim(q (ℓ ) , {e (ℓ ) 𝑑 } 𝑑 ∈𝐶 ℓ −1 ∩D 𝑖 )  . The final top-𝐾 results are drawn from 𝐶 ℓ final . Crucially, deeper levels refine the candidate set rather than restrict the final output size: the fi- nal answer always returns 𝐾 documents, but candidates are progres- sively re-scored at higher resolution. This progressive narrowing drastically reduces distance computations at finer resolutions. 3.7 Query-Adaptive Resolution Control SPI estimates query semantic uncertainty via entropy over attention- weighted components of q (1) : 𝐻 (q (1) ) = − 𝐷 1 ∑︁ 𝑘=1 𝑝 𝑘 log 𝑝 𝑘 , 𝑝 𝑘 = |𝑞 (1) 𝑘 | Í 𝑗 |𝑞 (1) 𝑗 | , where 𝑞 (1) 𝑘 is the 𝑘-th component of the ℓ 1 -normalized query embed- ding. The controller 𝑔 ctrl is a 2-layer Transformer with 128 hidden units and 4 attention heads: ˆ ℓ, 𝜎 ℓ = 𝑔 ctrl (q (1) , 𝐻 (q (1) )), outputting a predicted level ˆ ℓ ∈ {1, . . . , 𝐿} and a confidence score 𝜎 ℓ ∈ [0, 1]. Controller supervision and leakage prevention. Oracle labels ℓ ∗ 𝑞 are derived by binary search over levels on a dedicated label set disjoint from both training and evaluation data. Concretely, we split MS MARCO dev queries into three non-overlapping folds: 80% for controller training, 10% for oracle label generation (label set), and 10% as a held-out test set; oracle labels are never exposed to the model during training. The label ℓ ∗ 𝑞 = min{ℓ | Recall@100 (ℓ ) (𝑞) ≥ 0.99 · Recall@100 (𝐿) (𝑞)} depends on the document index, not on test queries. The controller is trained with cross-entropy on ℓ ∗ 𝑞 plus a temperature-scaled calibration term (temperature 𝑇 =1.2, tuned on the label set). Oracle level distribution on the label set: 45% at level 1, 32% at level 2, 23% at level 3. To assess OOD robustness, we evaluate the trained controller (without retraining) on BEIR-Quora and BEIR-FiQA, two domains absent from training. Controller accuracy (fraction of queries routed to oracle-optimal level) drops from 87.5% (in-domain) to 82.1% (OOD average), while the latency saving remains ≥ 3.8× vs. full-depth baseline—confirming that label artifacts do not explain the efficiency gains. Depth selection. The confidence threshold 𝜃 = 0.35 is tuned on a development set. Final depth follows: ℓ final = ( ˆ ℓ, 𝜎 ℓ ≤ 𝜃, min( ˆ ℓ + 1, 𝐿), otherwise. High-entropy queries (𝜎 ℓ > 𝜃 ) fall back to a deeper level, while confident predictions allow early termination. The controller is distinct from the progressive encoders and adds only 0.8 ms per query. 3.8 Streaming and Parallel Document Ingestion Offline construction vs. online streaming. It is important to dis- tinguish two operating regimes. In the offline steady state (all docu- ments fully processed), D (ℓ ) (𝑡) = D for every ℓ: all pyramid levels index the same corpus. This is the regime assumed by the recall analysis (Section 3.9) and by offline benchmarks. During online streaming, documents arrive faster than refinement encoders can process them, so the transient invariant is D (1) (𝑡) ⊇ D (2) (𝑡) ⊇ · · · ⊇ D (𝐿) (𝑡) at every wall-clock time 𝑡. The two statements are not contradictory: the steady-state claim is a convergence guaran- tee, not an instantaneous property. Level-wise insertion. SPI handles streaming inserts via on-demand level-wise insertion. Upon arrival of document 𝑑 at time 𝑡 arr 𝑑 : (1) Synchronous (level 1): e (1) 𝑑 is computed by the base encoder (tokenize → embed → normalize) and appended to I (1) . Docu- ment 𝑑 enters D (1) (𝑡) at 𝑡 = 𝑡 arr 𝑑 + 𝑇 (1) enc , where 𝑇 (1) enc is the base embedding latency (≈8 ms per passage at batch size 1). Because 𝑇 (1) enc is paid regardless of index depth, we call this the minimum insertion latency. (2) Asynchronous (levels ℓ ≥ 2): Refinement embeddings e (ℓ ) 𝑑 are computed in a background queue ordered by 𝑡 arr 𝑑 . Document 𝑑 enters D (ℓ ) (𝑡) at 𝑡 = 𝑡 arr 𝑑 +𝑇 (ℓ ) ins , where 𝑇 (ℓ ) ins = 𝑇 (1) enc +𝑂 (𝐷 ℓ /𝐵 enc ) and 𝐵 enc is encoder throughput (tokens/s). For queries issued while 𝑑 is partially available, the controller selects the deepest level ℓ ′ for which 𝑑 ∈ D (ℓ ′ ) (𝑡), returning a slightly coarser result rather than missing the document entirely. This graceful degradation ensures no document is invisible after its minimum insertion latency. Modern streaming ANN systems (IP-DiskANN [31], Quake [23], VStream [9]) focus on geometric freshness—graph edge repair and partition rebalancing under high update rates. SPI’s insertions are append-only (no structural repairs), which keeps per-insert latency low. The freshness tradeoff is explicit and bounded: level 1 is im- mediately consistent; level ℓ lags by 𝑇 (ℓ ) ins . Parallel execution. Each level I (ℓ ) is partitioned across 𝑁 nodes via LSH on level-1 embeddings. At each level, every node returns its local top-(𝑘 ℓ + 𝛿) candidates with boundary slack 𝛿 = ⌈𝑘 ℓ / √ 𝑁 ⌉; the coordinator merges and re-ranks to produce the global top-𝑘 ℓ . Candidate IDs are routed to deeper levels via a partition lookup table (document ID → LSH cell → node). LSH locality across levels is maintained because L cons bounds per-document embedding drift, limiting boundary leakage to 𝑂 (𝜀 ℓ /𝛿 2 LSH ) < 2%. Recall@10 drops by at most 0.6 points compared to a static index—well within the bounds of Theorem 1. Comparison with streaming ANN systems. We compare against IP-DiskANN [31] and Quake [23] on the same 1M-vector stream using SIFT-1M as a controlled benchmark. IP-DiskANN achieves higher geometric recall stability (recall@10 drop <0.1% after full turnover) but at 3.2× higher per-insert latency than SPI’s level-1 append, and does not support query-adaptive resolution. Quake adapts partitioning to query skew but also lacks multi- resolution semantic encoding. These systems and SPI address com- plementary problems and can be composed: SPI’s level-1 index could be backed by IP-DiskANN for maximum freshness at the coarsest granularity. 5 CONCLUSION We presented SPI, a query-adaptive multi-resolution indexing frame- work for streaming RAG in vector databases. By co-designing se- mantic pyramid encoding, uncertainty-aware depth control, and level-wise streaming insertion, SPI improves the efficiency–quality trade-off of ANN retrieval while remaining compatible with FAISS and Qdrant. Single-node experiments show a 1.4–2.3× average retrieval latency reduction under fixed Recall@10 targets, with competitive quality relative to comparable approximate-ANN base- lines. As RAG systems continue to scale, the cost of query and retrieval in VecDBs becomes time-expensive. SPI is an efficient solution to this challenge: by constructing a semantic pyramid and routing each query to the minimum representational depth sufficient for stable top-𝑘 retrieval, it substantially reduces average latency and memory pressure without a corresponding loss in recall. In future work, we will explore the principle underlying SPI—that index structure and representational depth need not be fixed at construction time—as a foundation for retrieval systems that remain both efficient and accurate as deployment conditions continue to evolve.
